The Malabar trevally (Platycaranx malabaricus) attains a maximum asymptotic body mass of approximately 3300 grams [Wwi = approximately 3300 grams], a figure derived from length-weight regressions applied to the species' ultimate total length. Field surveys and commercial catch data indicate that the largest individuals reach a total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], representing the ceiling of the species' size distribution in the wild. This length is notably consistent with the upper size range reported for other large-bodied carangids inhabiting coastal reef systems in the Indo-West Pacific. The body weight of a fish at the onset of reproductive maturity is considerably lower, with pubertal individuals typically weighing around 440 grams [Wwp = around 440 grams]. This substantial increase from maturity to maximum size reflects a prolonged phase of somatic growth that continues well after the reproductive system becomes functional, a life-history pattern frequently observed among iteroparous marine teleosts.

Sexual maturation in P. malabaricus occurs when individuals reach a total length of 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters], and this size threshold is accompanied by a marked increase in gonadal investment. Under environmental conditions typical of tropical reef waters (27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]), the gonadosomatic index (GSI) averages approximately 4.5% [GSI = approximately 4.5%]. This moderate index suggests a spawning strategy involving repeated events over an extended season rather than a single, catastrophic release of gametes. Morphometric data further indicate that the wet weight at puberty, estimated at 440 grams [Wwp = 440 grams], represents approximately thirteen percent of the ultimate wet weight, a ratio aligning with the broader carangid trend toward relatively late maturity in relation to maximal body size.

The early life stages of the Malabar trevally are characterized by a remarkably brief embryonic period. Eggs incubated at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C] hatch after approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days], a developmental duration that is typical for tropical carangids with small, pelagic eggs. The newly emerged larva carries a mass of only 0.000523 grams [Wwb = 0.000523 grams], a value calculated from a 1-millimeter egg diameter using the spherical volume formula. This negligible hatchling mass underscores the extreme fecundity required to offset high larval mortality in the planktonic environment. Upon yolk-sac resorption, the exotrophic larva must rapidly locate suitable prey to sustain the high growth rates necessary for survival through the early pelagic phase. The transition from the lecithotrophic to the exotrophic stage is a critical bottleneck that shapes subsequent recruitment success in this species.

Longevity records for P. malabaricus suggest a maximum lifespan of approximately 5475 days [am = approximately 5475 days] under the thermal regime of its native habitat (27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]). This translates to roughly 15 years, a moderate lifespan for a carangid of its size, placing it between the shorter-lived tropical jack species and the longer-lived temperate congeners. The age at birth of 8 days [ab = 8 days] represents a negligible fraction of the total lifespan, highlighting the species' reliance on high early mortality rather than extended parental investment at a temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. This life-history strategy is consistent with a Type III survivorship curve, where the vast majority of mortality occurs during the egg and larval stages, and only a tiny fraction of the cohort survives to reach the large adult sizes typical of the species.

Populations of P. malabaricus inhabiting different thermal regimes might exhibit subtle variation in these life-history parameters, but the values reported from the core of the species' range at 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C] provide a robust baseline. The gonadosomatic index was approximately 4.5% [GSI = approximately 4.5%] at a temperature of 27.5 °C [T = 27.5 °C]. The ultimate total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters] and the associated ultimate wet weight of approximately 3300 grams [Wwi = approximately 3300 grams] serve as key reference points for fisheries management, defining the upper size limit that the species can achieve under favorable conditions. Continued monitoring of these life-history parameters across the species' geographic range will be essential for understanding its resilience to environmental change and fishing pressure.
